title: Infinite Limits, Limits at Infinity, and Asymptotes
subject: AP Calculus AB

chunks.text: An infinite limit occurs when, as x approaches a finite value a, the function's outputs grow without bound toward positive or negative infinity. Infinite limits correspond to vertical asymptotes.

A limit at infinity asks what value a function approaches as the input x runs off toward positive or negative infinity. Limits at infinity describe end behavior and correspond to horizontal asymptotes.

In an infinite limit the infinity appears in the answer because the output blows up, while in a limit at infinity the infinity appears in the question because the input runs away. The two produce vertical and horizontal asymptotes respectively.
Infinity is not a real number. Writing that a limit equals infinity means the function grows without bound; it is a precise description of how the limit fails to be finite, not a numerical value.

A vertical asymptote of a rational function occurs at an x-value where the denominator equals zero but the numerator does not. Values that make both numerator and denominator zero are removable holes, not asymptotes.

To determine whether an infinite limit is positive or negative, do a sign analysis: pick a test value just to the left and just to the right of the asymptote and track the sign of the numerator divided by the tiny denominator.
For f(x) = 1/x near x = 0, the limit from the right is positive infinity and the limit from the left is negative infinity, so the one-sided infinite limits have opposite signs.

When the two one-sided infinite limits at a vertical asymptote have opposite signs, the two-sided limit does not exist, although each one-sided limit can be precisely described as plus or minus infinity.

A linear factor like (x - 3) in a denominator changes sign as x crosses 3, so the two sides of that asymptote usually go to opposite infinities. A squared factor like (x - 3)² stays positive, so both sides go to the same infinity.
For f(x) = 1/(x - 4)², the denominator is always positive, so the function approaches positive infinity from both sides and the two-sided limit is positive infinity.

The notation lim(x→∞) f(x) = L means that as x grows without bound, the function values get arbitrarily close to L. The function may never reach L but approaches it as far out along the x-axis as desired.
Key building-block limits at infinity: lim(x→∞) 1/x = 0, lim(x→∞) 1/xⁿ = 0 for any positive n, lim(x→∞) c = c for a constant c, and lim(x→∞) xⁿ = ∞ for positive n.
For a rational function as x approaches infinity, only the highest-degree term in the numerator and the highest-degree term in the denominator matter; all lower-degree terms become negligible.
Degree comparison rule, case 1: if the numerator's degree is less than the denominator's degree, the limit at infinity is 0. Example: lim(x→∞) (2x + 1)/(x³ - 5) = 0.
Degree comparison rule, case 2: if the numerator and denominator have equal degree, the limit at infinity equals the ratio of the leading coefficients. Example: lim(x→∞) (3x² + 2x)/(5x² - 4) = 3/5.

Degree comparison rule, case 3: if the numerator's degree is greater than the denominator's degree, the function grows without bound and the limit at infinity is positive or negative infinity. Example: lim(x→∞) (x³ + 1)/(2x + 7) = ∞.

The divide-by-highest-power method evaluates a limit at infinity by dividing every term in the numerator and denominator by the highest power of x in the denominator, then sending each remaining constant-over-power term to zero.
A horizontal asymptote is the line y = L when lim(x→∞) f(x) = L or lim(x→-∞) f(x) = L. A function can have zero, one, or two horizontal asymptotes.

A function can cross its horizontal asymptote. For example, sin(x)/x oscillates across the line y = 0 infinitely often while still approaching 0 in the long run. A horizontal asymptote describes only end behavior.
A vertical asymptote cannot be crossed because the function blows up there, while a horizontal asymptote can be crossed because it only describes the function's behavior as x approaches infinity.
When evaluating limits as x approaches negative infinity, even powers such as x² and x⁴ stay positive while odd powers such as x, x³, and x⁵ become negative, which can flip the sign of the result.

The hierarchy of growth from slowest to fastest is logarithmic ln(x), then polynomial xⁿ with higher degree faster, then exponential aˣ for a greater than 1. In a competing ratio at infinity, the faster-growing function dominates.
Because exponentials outgrow polynomials, lim(x→∞) x¹⁰⁰/2ˣ = 0, and because polynomials outgrow logarithms, lim(x→∞) ln(x)/x = 0.

Example of finding a vertical asymptote with signs: for f(x) = (x + 2)/(x - 3), the asymptote is at x = 3; from the right the limit is +∞ and from the left it is -∞, so the two-sided limit does not exist.
